From LLM to LAM: Large Action Models

From generating answers to choosing, executing and verifying actions.

Browse all 13 slides

From saying to doing

This presentation explains action-oriented AI through definitions, an execution loop, a document-editing example and a model-training case study. It follows the progression from language generation and function calling to agent frameworks and models trained on action trajectories.

The term LAM is used in different ways. The deck distinguishes model training from the surrounding execution system, and emphasizes grounding, permissions, observability and task-level evaluation.

What an action-oriented system must do

CapabilityPurpose
IntentUnderstand the user’s goal and current environment
PlanningChoose the next operation or sequence of steps
ExecutionRun a permitted GUI operation, API call or command
ObservationCheck whether the operation achieved its intended result
AdaptationRecover, re-plan or stop based on the observed state
EvaluationMeasure completion, action correctness, latency and safety

What Is a Large Action Model?

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Large Action Models · From LLM to LAM What is a Large Action Model? A model — usually an LLM further trained on action data — that turns a user's intent into a sequence of executable actions in a digital or physical environment, observes what happened, and adapts until the task is done. Interprets intent Infers the real goal from text, voice, screenshots or video — including what is only implied. Generates actions Emits GUI operations, API calls, code or robot commands instead of prose. Plans and adapts Breaks a task into steps and re-plans when an action fails or the screen changes. Specializes Often smaller than general LLMs, tuned to a domain where it can match or beat them. 2

LLM vs. LAM at a Glance

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Large Action Models · From LLM to LAM LLM vs LAM at a glance LLM — Large Language Model LAM — Large Action Model Primary output Text, code, answers Executable actions: clicks, keystrokes, API calls, code Environment Static: prompt in, response out Dynamic: apps, operating systems, web, devices Loop One pass; a human acts on the answer Closed loop: act → observe → adapt → act Success measured by Accuracy and quality of text Task completion, steps, latency and safety Scope and size General-purpose and very large Often smaller and specialized to a domain Typical failure A wrong answer (hallucination) A wrong action with real side effects 3

The Path from LLM to LAM

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Large Action Models · From LLM to LAM The path from LLM to LAM 1 LLM Text in, text out. Answers, drafts and code — a human takes the action. Chat assistants 2 Function calling The model emits a structured (JSON) call for a tool; the application executes it. Tool-use APIs 3 Agent frameworks A runtime wraps the LLM in a loop with memory, tools and planning (ReAct-style). LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK 4 LAM The model is trained on action trajectories: it plans, acts, observes and recovers natively. xLAM, UFO LAM, computer-use models More autonomy · tighter coupling to the environment · higher stakes per mistake 4

The Action Loop

Large Action Models · From LLM to LAM How a LAM works: the action loop Perceive screen, UI tree, API state Plan choose the next step Act click · type · call API Observe check result, catch errors LAM goal: user intent The agent system around the model Action executor turns model output into real clicks and API calls Memory past steps, task state, user context Environment interface screenshots, accessibility tree, APIs Guardrails validation, approvals, stop rules, rollback 5

Slide 6 of 13

Instructions vs. Executed Actions

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Large Action Models · From LLM to LAM Same request, two very different outputs Request: “In report.docx, make the title bold and insert a table of contents.” LLM: instructions for a human Sure! Here's how: 1. Open report.docx in Word. 2. Select the title and press Ctrl+B. 3. Place the cursor below the title. 4. Choose References → Table of Contents. Outcome: nothing changes until you do it. LAM: actions executed in the app open_app("Word", file="report.docx") select(control="Title") click(control="Bold") set_cursor(after="Title") click("References > Table of Contents") observe() → TOC present ✓ Outcome: the document is changed — and verified. 6
Back to slide navigation

Slide 7 of 13

A Five-Stage Building Pipeline

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Large Action Models · From LLM to LAM Building a LAM: a five-stage pipeline 1 Data collection Gather task-plan pairs and task-action trajectories; evolve them into harder tasks. 2 Model training Fine-tune an LLM in phases: plans first, then actions, then reinforcement learning. 3 Offline evaluation Score plans and action steps against held-out trajectories. 4 Integration and grounding Wire the model into an agent: executor, memory, UI and API interface. 5 Online evaluation Run real tasks live; measure success rate, steps and latency. Case study: Microsoft built a LAM for its UFO Windows agent and tested it on Microsoft Word tasks (Wang et al., 2024). 7

Four Training Phases

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Large Action Models · From LLM to LAM Turning an LLM into a LAM: four training phases 1 Task-plan pretraining 76,672 task → plan pairs teach a Mistral-7B base to break requests into steps. 2 Learning from experts Imitates 2,192 successful GPT-4o action trajectories. 3 Self-boosting exploration Retries 2,284 tasks GPT-4o failed; keeps 496 new successes. 4 Reward model + offline PPO Learns from 1,788 failed trajectories using a learned reward. 8

Interpreting the Case-Study Results

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Large Action Models · From LLM to LAM Results: a small LAM beats a frontier LLM in its domain Task success rate 71.0% vs 63.0% for GPT-4o Time to complete a task 30.4 s vs 86.4 s for GPT-4o Latency per step 5.4 s vs 12.8 s for GPT-4o Read it carefully. Live test on 435 Word requests, text-only input. GPT-4o given screenshots too reached 75.5% success but took 96.5 s per task. The win is near-frontier accuracy at a fraction of the time — inside the one app the LAM was trained for. 9

The LAM Landscape

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Large Action Models · From LLM to LAM Who is building LAMs Rabbit Consumer · UI navigation Coined “Large Action Model” with the r1 device (2024): a model meant to learn and operate app interfaces for the user. Salesforce xLAM Enterprise · function calling Open model family tuned for function calling, reasoning and planning; topped the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard. Microsoft UFO LAM Research · desktop GUI A 7B model trained in four phases to operate Windows apps; beat GPT-4o on success and speed in Word. Frontier and enterprise agents Production · tools + computer use General models now ship native tool and computer use; vendors such as Genesys market LAM-powered agents (Feb 2026). A word on the label There is no strict industry definition. “LAM” describes both models trained on action data and LLMs wired to tools. Judge by behavior: does it choose, execute and verify actions — and can you audit it? 10

Challenges and Guardrails

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Large Action Models · From LLM to LAM Challenges and guardrails Real side effects Actions send, buy and delete. Validate before executing; design approvals and rollback. Environment drift A software update or moved button can break a learned policy. Plan for re-grounding. Costly training data Domain trajectories are expensive to collect; synthetic and self-generated data help. Latency and cost Multi-step loops multiply model calls; smaller specialized LAMs cut per-step latency. Accountability Who owns a harmful action? Finance, healthcare and transport need rules and audit trails. Evaluate the trajectory Score tool choice, arguments, order, safety and completion — not just the final text. 11

Key Takeaways

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Key takeaways 1 An LLM generates language; a LAM completes tasks by choosing, executing and verifying actions. 2 The path runs LLM → function calling → agent frameworks → models trained on action trajectories. 3 Specialized LAMs can beat larger general models on success and speed — inside their domain. 4 Shipping a LAM is a systems problem: grounding, guardrails, rollback and trajectory-level evaluation. 12

Reading the case study

The source reports 71.0% task success for a specialized model on 435 Word requests, compared with 63.0% for the text-only GPT-4o comparator. It also reports that a screenshot-enabled GPT-4o comparator reached 75.5%. These are results from the cited study as presented in the deck, not a current general-purpose model ranking.

Frequently asked questions

What is a Large Action Model?

The deck describes a model that translates user intent into executable actions, observes the results and adapts toward task completion. It also notes that LAM has no strict industry-wide definition.

How does a LAM differ from an LLM?

The presentation contrasts language output with action-oriented behavior. These categories overlap: LLMs can participate in tool-using agent systems, while some models are further trained on action trajectories.

What components surround the action model?

The deck identifies an action executor, memory, an environment interface and guardrails. Together they support a perceive, plan, act and observe loop.

Do the case-study results show that LAMs are better at every task?

No. The reported comparison concerns a specialized model evaluated on 435 Microsoft Word requests. The deck distinguishes text-only results from a screenshot-enabled comparator. These results should not be generalized beyond the evaluated setting.

Can rollback undo every action?

No. Restoring configuration or application state cannot necessarily undo an external message, completed transaction or disclosed information. Approvals and action limits are important before consequential execution.
